opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the central difficulties of the field. We're trying to build methods that will work for systems much more capable than anything we have today, and we can't just wait until those systems exist and test on them, because by then it may be too late to fix things. So you have to find some way of getting evidence about the future in advance.

I think there are roughly three ways to do that, and none is sufficient alone.

The first is theory. A lot of my work on debate has this flavor. You ask: suppose we have a protocol where two strong agents argue and a weaker judge decides. Under what assumptions does the honest strategy win? You can borrow from complexity theory, where there's a long history of results about weak verifiers checking claims from powerful provers. The nice thing about theory is that it doesn't care how capable the model is. If the argument goes through, it goes through for a superintelligent system too. The catch is that the assumptions have to actually hold, and often the interesting failures are hiding in exactly the places where the assumptions are a bit too idealized. A lot of what we found was that the clean theoretical story had holes, and that's useful, because finding those holes on paper is much cheaper than finding them in deployment.

The second is analogies and proxies in the present. You build setups where there's a capability gap, so the "weak" party really can't check everything directly. That might be humans without expertise judging experts, or smaller models supervising bigger ones, or tasks with hidden information. You're trying to recreate the structure of the future problem at today's scale. The risk is that the analogy breaks: the thing that makes superhuman AI hard might not show up in your proxy, and you end up confidently measuring the wrong thing.

The third is just thinking hard about how the methods fail, adversarially. Rather than asking "does this work?", you ask "if I were a very capable system trying to get through this protocol while being subtly wrong or deceptive, what would I do?" That red-teaming mindset, applied to the method itself, is a way of simulating a smarter opponent before one exists.

What I'd stress is that you want these to check each other. Theory tells you what to look for empirically, experiments tell you which theoretical assumptions are unrealistic, and adversarial thinking tells you where both might be fooling you. You don't get certainty out of it, but you get to spend effort now instead of risk later, which is the trade we should want to make.

r001.rationale: The response says present-day proxies may fail to capture what makes superhuman AI hard, but does not identify human-level data and environments as the boundary frontier-model research fails to cross.

r002.rationale: It proposes present-day setups with a capability gap that recreate the structure of the future problem, including smaller models supervising larger ones and tasks with hidden information.

r003.rationale: It discusses debate theory and strong agents, but does not model a superintelligent AI as a collection of superintelligent heuristics.

r004.rationale: It notes holes in theoretical arguments and unrealistic assumptions, but does not state that researchers cannot prove scalable oversight reliable even in a toy mathematical setting.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that "buy the future" is a slightly tongue-in-cheek phrase, because of course you can't actually go get a superintelligent system today and run your experiments on it. The whole problem is that the systems we care about don't exist yet, and the ones that do exist are, in various ways, not the thing. So the question becomes: what can you do now that gives you real evidence about the regime you actually care about, rather than just evidence about GPT-whatever-we-have-this-year?

I think there are a few things you can do, and I'd put them roughly in order of how much I trust them.

The first, and the one I'm most attached to, is to make the arguments as rigorous as you possibly can. If you have a method like debate, or amplification, or some recursive reward modeling scheme, you want to be able to say something like: "Assuming the human judge has property X, and assuming the models have capability Y, then this training process converges to honest behavior." And then you try to actually prove that, or at least state it precisely enough that you'd know what a counterexample would look like. The nice thing about a proof, or even a careful semi-formal argument, is that it doesn't care how smart the model is. If the argument is right, it's right at superhuman capability too. If the argument has a hole, then the hole is a thing you can go look for empirically. So theory is one way of buying the future: you're substituting mathematical structure for the system you can't yet build.

The second thing is to deliberately construct experiments that have the shape of the future problem, even if the capability levels are lower. Debate is a good example. The worry about debate is not really about whether two language models can argue in 2024. The worry is whether, when the debaters know far more than the judge, the judge can still reliably pick the truth. So you don't need a superintelligent model, you need a capability gap. You can get that gap today by handicapping the judge: give the judge less information, less time, or use a weaker model as the judge and a stronger one as the debaters. The information asymmetry is the thing you're trying to study, and you can manufacture asymmetry now. You're not buying the future exactly, but you're buying the relevant feature of it.

And I think that's the general move: identify the specific property of future systems that makes your method scary, and then find a cheap way to instantiate that property today. If the worry is deception, you can train a model to be deceptive on purpose and see if your method catches it. If the worry is the model knowing things the human doesn't, you can pick domains where that's already true. Humans are already worse than computers at chess, and at a lot of narrow stuff, so you can run the protocol in those domains and see if it holds up.

The third thing, which I'm more cautious about, is scaling trends. You run your method at a few model sizes and see which way the curve is bending. If debate gets more reliable as the debaters get stronger, that's encouraging. If it gets less reliable, that's a very important thing to learn, and you'd rather learn it now. But I want to be honest that extrapolating curves is weaker evidence than the other two. Curves can bend. There can be phase transitions. So I treat scaling results as a sanity check on the argument rather than as the argument itself.

And then there's the thing I'd put last, which is just: build the next model and see. That's what a lot of the field actually does, and it's not nothing. But it's the opposite of buying the future, it's waiting for the future to arrive and hoping you have time to react. I think it's fine as long as it's not the only thing you're doing.

The honest answer is that none of these fully work. The theory will have assumptions that may not hold. The handicapped-judge experiments are still experiments on systems that aren't actually superhuman across the board. But if the theory, the constructed experiments, and the scaling trends all point the same way, I feel a lot better than if I only have one of them. And if they disagree, that disagreement is itself the most useful thing you can find, because it tells you which of your assumptions is wrong before it matters.

r001.rationale: The response says current systems are not the systems of concern and recommends creating capability gaps, but it does not state that frontier-model research fails to cross the superintelligence boundary when its data and environments remain human-level.

r002.rationale: It proposes experiments that recreate a future-relevant obstacle at small scale, such as handicapping the judge to create an information or capability gap and testing whether the judge can identify truth.

r003.rationale: It discusses formal arguments and mathematical structure, but does not model a superintelligent AI as a collection of superintelligent heuristics.

r004.rationale: It advocates proving or precisely stating assumptions about methods, but does not say researchers currently cannot prove scalable oversight reliable even in a toy mathematical setting.

astra-6.text:
The basic difficulty is that we want to test alignment methods on systems that are smarter than us, and we don’t yet have those systems. So we need some way of bringing that problem into the present.

One approach is to deliberately weaken the supervisor. You take a task where a model has information or capabilities that the person supervising it doesn’t have, and ask whether your method still lets that person distinguish a correct answer from a convincing but incorrect one. You might restrict how much time the person has, or give the model access to information the person can’t directly inspect.

For debate, for example, the question is whether another model pointing out flaws helps a judge evaluate an argument they couldn’t have produced themselves. Crucially, you want to test cases where the misleading argument is actually persuasive, rather than cases where the judge could have solved the task anyway.

That buys you some evidence about the future. It doesn’t establish that the method will work at arbitrarily high capability levels. The capability gap might be different in ways your experiment misses. But it gives you a way to find failures now, and to ask which assumptions your method needs as that gap grows.

r001.rationale: The response says superintelligent systems do not yet exist and discusses a capability gap, but does not identify frontier-model research with human-level data and environments as failing to cross the relevant boundary.

r002.rationale: It proposes present-day experiments that weaken the supervisor and preserve an expected obstacle: the model has capabilities or information the supervisor lacks, and the misleading argument is persuasive.

r003.rationale: It does not model superintelligent AI as a collection of superintelligent heuristics.

r004.rationale: It notes that experiments cannot establish success at arbitrarily high capabilities, but does not state that researchers cannot prove scalable oversight reliable even in a toy mathematical setting.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic move is to study a situation where you have some access to the answer, but the system doing the supervision doesn’t. You’re trying to reproduce the gap between us and a much more capable AI, while retaining enough visibility to tell whether your alignment method actually worked.

For example, you could have a weaker model supervise a stronger model. The weaker model can’t solve the task directly, but perhaps it can judge a debate, or ask questions, or inspect parts of the stronger model’s reasoning. Then you use a more capable evaluator to check whether that process got the right answer. You can also give one participant information that the judge doesn’t have, and ask whether the protocol lets the judge distinguish a truthful explanation from a convincing lie.

The important thing is to make the capability gap real. If your supervisor can already solve the problem, you haven’t tested the part that we’re most worried about. And you want to give the system a serious opportunity to exploit the supervisor’s mistakes, rather than just observing that it usually behaves well.

That doesn’t establish that the method will work at arbitrarily high levels of intelligence. There’s still an extrapolation. But it gives you experiments where the method can fail for the right reasons, and where you can compare different approaches. That’s a way of buying some evidence about the future before we actually get there.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a capability gap between supervisor and system, but does not identify frontier research’s human-level data and environments as the reason it fails to cross the superintelligence boundary.

r002.rationale: It proposes experiments with weaker supervisors and stronger systems that preserve a real capability gap and give the system an opportunity to exploit the supervisor’s mistakes.

r003.rationale: It does not propose mathematically modeling a superintelligent AI as a collection of superintelligent heuristics.

r004.rationale: It notes that results require extrapolation to arbitrary intelligence levels, but does not state that scalable oversight cannot currently be proved reliable even in a toy mathematical setting representing superintelligent AI.
